questions.question: Explain the two doors of population change and the four stages of the demographic cycle, placing South Africa.
questions.expected_answer: Population changes through natural growth (births minus deaths, expressed per thousand) and migration (arrivals minus departures). The cycle: high stationary — high births and deaths, little growth; early expanding — death rates fall (water, vaccines, medicine) while births stay high: rapid growth; late expanding — birth rates fall too (urbanisation, education especially of women, family planning): growth slows; low stationary — low births and deaths, stable or declining population. South Africa sits in the later expanding phase: young population, growth continuing but slowing, with internal migration toward metropolitan cores and international migration in both directions.

questions.question: Define the nested labour-market terms and both unemployment definitions, with the two key rates and their denominators.
questions.expected_answer: Population → working-age population (15–64) → labour force: the employed plus the strictly unemployed (without work, available, actively seeking). Outside stand learners, homemakers, the ill — and discouraged work-seekers, who want work but stopped searching: excluded by the strict definition, included by the expanded one, a gap of several percentage points in South Africa. The unemployment rate = unemployed ÷ labour force (never the population); the participation rate = labour force ÷ working-age population. SA's profile: young labour force, youth unemployment far above the national rate, jobs concentrated in metros with former homeland areas carrying heavy rates.

questions.question: Describe the labour market's demand and supply, the meaning of derived demand, and the skills-divided market.
questions.expected_answer: Households supply labour; firms demand it; the wage is the price. Demand is DERIVED — firms want workers for the output they produce, so labour demand follows the demand for goods, rising in booms and falling in downswings; it slopes downward in the wage as firms substitute machines or cut output. Supply slopes upward: better pay draws more seekers and hours. The market splits by skill: scarce skills see demand outrun supply (high wages, unfilled posts); unskilled labour sees supply flood demand (pressed wages, long queues). The skills mismatch — too few trained for what firms seek, too many offering what they need less — is the structural heart of SA unemployment; training is the ticket between the gates.
